title: Where can the ISS fly over?
hook: The space station circles the Earth again and again. Does it visit every city?

knows: the ISS circles the Earth about every 90 minutes
doesNotKnow: that a satellite's track only covers a band of latitudes
what orbital tilt means for ground coverage

misconception: Over days, the ISS passes over every city on Earth.
objective: The learner can say that a satellite's ground track reaches latitudes up to its orbital tilt and no further, so the ISS at 51.6 degrees reaches London but not Moscow.

claims.text: The ISS orbit is tilted 51.6 degrees to the equator.
claims.source: NASA, 'International Space Station orbit' / ISS fact sheets: inclination 51.64 degrees (cited from memory by the builder, not re-fetched). Rounded to 51.6.

claims.text: A circular orbit tilted 51.6 degrees carries the satellite to 51.6 degrees north and south and no farther.
claims.source: On a spherical Earth the maximum latitude of the ground track equals the inclination (for inclinations up to 90): sin(lat) = sin(i) sin(u). The stage draws the track from exactly this formula. On the real, slightly flattened Earth the geodetic latitude differs by about 0.2 degrees (brief; from memory, not displayed).

claims.text: London (51.5 N) sits just inside the limit; Moscow (55.8 N) is about 460 km farther north, outside it.
claims.source: City latitudes from a gazetteer (from memory): London 51.5074, Moscow 55.7558, Rome 41.9028. (55.7558 - 51.6) x 111.2 km/degree = 462 km, shown as about 460; London is 10 km inside the 51.6 limit (node, scratch script).

claims.text: You needed a tilt near 56 degrees to reach Moscow.
claims.source: The milestone fires at a tilt of at least Moscow's latitude, 55.76 degrees; the reveal rounds up to 56.

claims.text: Reaching a latitude is not the same as passing over a city on a given day: that also depends on timing.
claims.source: The ground track shifts westward each lap as the Earth turns (the stage draws 23 degrees per lap), so which longitudes are crossed on a given day depends on the orbit's phase.

claims.text: Idealised circular orbit, three laps (the stage's track assumes a circular orbit and the Earth turning 23 degrees per lap).
claims.source: A model label for the stage. 23 degrees is 360 x (about 92 min) / 1,436 min; the ISS lap time of about 92 minutes is cited from memory (NASA).

claims.text: The ISS circles the Earth about every 90 minutes.
claims.source: Hook-level fact on the 'learner knows' list (the hook says 'again and again'). NASA ISS fact sheets: about 92 minutes per orbit (from memory).

recall.question: A satellite's orbit is tilted 30 degrees to the equator. What is the farthest north its ground track can reach?
options: All the way to the North Pole
recall.why: The ground track reaches latitudes up to the orbit's tilt and then turns back, so a 30 degree tilt means 30 degrees north and south.
